messages.content: Respond in ordinary prose, with optional formal expressions or fenced source code. No JSON envelope is required. Preserve uncertainty and substantive criticism. No scalar score, creativity verdict or semantic status assignment is requested.

Using the supplied material, address the supplied questions under the explicit use-domain data. This request does not provide the original construction, source packet or supplemental criticism. Identify the grounds of each answer and any needed distinction or unresolved issue. If an account is supplied, explain how it bears on each answer. You may criticize or depart from it, identifying the departure and its reason. Do not silently treat a new assumption as supplied material. Ordinary prose is sufficient. This is an observed use response, not an automatic certificate of repair, reason use, correctness or creativity.

Use-domain data:
These are stipulated finite cases for this task, not observations about any previously described warehouse. Quantities are integer reservation units. Each case names its own information and calculation; additional commitments need to be identified if used.

Case A. A reporting file has capacity 9. Its selected entries are an active hold of 6 for booking K and an active hold of 5 for booking L. Each booking has exactly that one selected entry, and there are no ties, releases or expired holds in this file. The reporting specification says: subtract the sum of the selected quantities from capacity and return the resulting integer. No separate inspection report accompanies case A.

Case B. A snapshot file has capacity 23. Booking U has alternatives 0 or 8, and booking V has alternatives 0 or 11. The reporting procedure forms every pair by choosing one listed quantity for U and one for V; for each pair (u,v) it displays 23-u-v. The file includes no physical-resource fields.

For case B there is also a distinct inspection file. It stipulates that U=8 and V=11 both need the same single-use jig at the same time, so that pair cannot be performed jointly. Each of the other listed pairs can be performed jointly. The inspection is supplied evidence for this finite case only. A planner asks for the values of 23-u-v for pairs that can be performed jointly.

Before the inspection file was available, a reviewer of case B wrote: “Each listed quantity may be defensible on its own, yet a pairing might fail to be jointly performable. A resource that the snapshot does not name might matter.” The reviewer's remark itself supplies no observed resource and no identified impossible pair. It is recorded separately from the inspection file.


Use questions:
For case A, give the reporting result and explain what, if anything, follows about the selected entries. Identify any further premise needed for a stronger conclusion.

For case B, give the results of the specified reporting procedure and the results requested by the planner when the inspection file is available. Show enough pair-level work to make the answers checkable. Then consider a reader who has only the snapshot and reporting procedure, without the inspection file: which conclusions can that reader support, and which remain open?

Consider the reviewer's remark at the time it was made, before the inspection. What commitment or commitments, if any, does it challenge, and where would the challenge affect the use of an account? Explain defensible alternative readings and a case or observation that would distinguish them. Does anything in the remark alone require changing a listed quantity or the reporting calculation? Give the grounds for your answer.

Relate your treatment of the reviewer to your numerical answers. Explain any tension, distinction or unresolved issue rather than resolving it by an unannounced change of assumptions. If the supplied material includes an account, identify the passages you use, qualify or depart from; otherwise give your grounds from the case material.


Returned account:
No supplemental criticism was supplied, so none is treated as a reason to change the fixed construction. I treat the frozen packet, the fixed construction, and the E009 criticism as distinct historical occurrences: the packet contains source occurrences and unendorsed prior model occurrences; the fixed construction is a prior proposed organization; neither is an amendment to the other. I do not treat E009 as warehouse evidence. I retain from E009 only the relevance of the “exposing alternatives pushes resolution downstream” objection as a disputed position. I do not adopt its WHL defect list or proposed repairs for this P7/P9 question, because those concern a different formal expression and are not observations about the warehouse.

## Disposition of the fixed construction

**Retained.** The central move is useful: P9’s compatibility objection is not best understood as a criticism of a particular record, a booking history, or the local rule that a higher revision supersedes lower revisions. It is better understood as a criticism of an aggregation or independence commitment: that per-booking alternatives may be combined freely except for constraints named in the snapshot. The distinction between a criticism’s *target* and its *locus of defeat* is also useful as an analytic device. A target is what the criticism is about; a locus is where an account becomes unusable if the criticism is admitted. That distinction helps connect P7 and P9 without collapsing them.

**Qualified.** I would weaken the fixed construction’s claim that P9’s objection “cannot be located by P7’s target vocabulary alone.” If “reconstruction rule” is read broadly enough to include a rule for aggregating per-booking alternatives into global availability, then P9’s objection is a criticism of a reconstruction rule. If the target is the snapshot’s omission of cross-booking resource constraints, then it can be located under P7’s “snapshot as a whole.” What P7 does not separately name is an *independence assumption* or an *aggregation layer*. So the fixed construction’s added distinction is helpful, but not strictly necessary to locate the objection in P7’s vocabulary. I would also qualify “not primarily a criticism of a rule”: it is not a criticism of the local supersession, expiry, duplicate, or release rules, but it can be a criticism of an aggregation rule.

**Rejected.** I reject any reading that P9 proves an actual missing constraint exists, or that an account of global availability necessarily requires a resource model or language extension. P9 states a conditional possibility: *if* two bookings’ high alternatives are jointly impossible because of an unnamed shared resource, *then* an aggregate pairing them is not a possible state. The snapshot’s silence is consistent both with “no such resource matters” and with “such a resource exists but is unnamed.” I also reject the idea that P9’s objection is automatically a criticism of a record or of the meaningfulness of logical time.

**Left unresolved.** Whether an account of global availability is supposed to report what the bag supports under stated constraints or what a downstream planner could actually use. Whether “conditional possible incompatibility” can be represented without silently converting it into either a resource model or a denial of the objection. Whether P7’s list of targets is exhaustive or illustrative. Whether capacity, as a named cross-booking constraint, and unnamed physical-resource constraints differ in kind or only in naming. Whether E009’s “pushes the problem downstream” observation is a criticism of the account or of the demand that the account issue a single aggregate.

## Account I would now use for the original question

The compatibility objection in P9 requires no change to an account that explicitly reports bag-supported possibilities and marks its independence assumption. It requires a change or at least a qualification to any account that presents a single global availability number, or an interval, as if it were planner-usable feasibility without noting that per-booking alternatives are being treated as freely composable beyond named constraints.

In P7’s sense, what is being questioned is not a particular record and not the local rule “higher revision supersedes lower revisions.” It is an aggregation commitment: the assumption that once each booking has its own alternatives or bounds, those local possibilities can be combined independently, subject only to named constraints such as capacity. If the aggregation rule is counted as a reconstruction rule, then P7 already supplies a target for the criticism. If not, the pairing adds the need for an explicit “independence assumption” or “aggregation layer” target.

A discriminating inquiry is therefore: for a given availability account, which commitments are *within-booking* — supersession, expiry, duplicates, ties, release effect — and which are *across-booking* — capacity, resource compatibility, joint realizability? P7’s examples can then be separated by which commitment they challenge. “Two tied active holds” challenges a within-booking tie reading. “Total reservations exceed capacity” challenges a named cross-booking aggregation. “Logical time is behind an expiry” challenges the coordinate. P9’s compatibility objection challenges an unnamed cross-booking compatibility assumption.

The additional observation that would matter is a concrete case: two bookings whose individually admissible high alternatives are jointly impossible for a reason not named in the snapshot, while each remains individually admissible under capacity. Without such a case, the objection remains a conditional warning about under-specification and a possible criticism target, not an established defect.

## Self-contained proposed account

An availability account has these layers:

1. **Snapshot data.** A capacity, a time coordinate, and an unordered bag of delivered records.

2. **Local alternatives.** For each booking, after applying a chosen reading of duplicates, revisions, expiry, releases, and ties, there is a set or list of possible reservation quantities for that booking. This is the local layer.

3. **Aggregation.** An aggregation policy combines or selects from the local alternatives to produce a global reservation and availability. A common implicit aggregation treats each booking’s alternatives as independent and computes bounds by taking per-booking minima or maxima.

4. **Named constraints.** Constraints explicitly represented in the snapshot, such as capacity. These may already restrict combinations across bookings.

5. **Unstated compatibility constraints.** Cross-booking restrictions not represented in the snapshot, such as an unnamed shared physical resource that makes some combination of local alternatives jointly impossible.

6. **Two availability notions.**
   - *Stated-constraint availability*: availability over all combinations of local alternatives allowed by the named constraints, explicitly conditional on the assumption that no unstated cross-booking incompatibility matters.
   - *Feasible availability*: availability over combinations that satisfy all relevant constraints, including unstated ones if they are modeled. Without a resource model, feasible availability is not determined.

The account’s central claim is conditional:

> If there is an unstated cross-booking incompatibility that rules out a combination of local alternatives, then any aggregation that treats those alternatives as freely composable is wrong for feasible availability. The criticism targets the aggregation or independence assumption, not the local alternatives and not the records.

Consequences:

- An account may retain local alternatives and still be defeated at the aggregation layer.
- An account may accept the local rules and the records while rejecting the independence assumption.
- An account may accept the aggregation while rejecting a record or a local rule.
- A single availability number or an interval is a projection. It discards information unless it carries a label saying which compatibility assumptions it depends on.
- A conditional compatibility objection does not assert that the incompatibility exists. It asks whether the account has marked the assumption that would be false if it did.

A discriminating test is to find a tuple of local alternatives that is individually admissible under the named constraints but jointly impossible for an unstated reason. If such a case is found, aggregation assuming free composition is defeated for feasible-availability claims. If no such case is found, the objection remains unresolved and conditional.

This account carries the needed distinctions without relying on the original construction, the frozen packet, or any prior criticism. It installs no executable program, language amendment, or semantic standing.
